claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its high-entropy-alloy derivatives exhibit coercivity below or equal to 100 Oe.
A minor Al addition followed by an appropriate heat treatment will induce controlled nanoscale precipitation in an otherwise single-phase fcc FeCoNi-based alloy.
Al is an element that can promote formation of a multiphase, precipitate-containing microstructure.
The intervention will produce coherent nanoscale secondary-phase precipitates embedded in an fcc matrix.
The precipitates can be formed with a narrow size distribution and low volume fraction.
Maintaining a low precipitate volume fraction will preserve the alloy's overall saturation magnetization.
Coherent nanoscale precipitates will act as magnetic domain-wall pinning sites.
Pinning by the precipitates will hinder domain-wall motion during magnetization reversal.
Hindering domain-wall motion will increase the coercive field.
The Al-modified and precipitation-treated alloy will have significantly higher coercivity than the matched single-phase fcc control.
The increase in coercivity is expected to be appreciable, although its magnitude is not specified.
The intervention should avoid a drastic change in the overall alloy composition or phase fraction.
Magnetic properties should be measured at room temperature under conditions comparable to those used for the control.
TEM and EDS will be used to determine whether precipitates form and to characterize their size, distribution, and composition.
Magnetometry will compare coercivity and saturation magnetization between the modified alloy and a matched control.
The hypothesis will be falsified if precipitates are absent or if the modified sample shows no statistically significant coercivity increase beyond measurement error or a pre-defined threshold.
